title: The order of the upload log lines
scenario: upload() logs each step and fails on an empty file. The caller catches the failure. Predict the exact log.
question: What does this print?
options:
start
cleanup
caught empty
done

start
caught empty
cleanup
done

start
sent
cleanup
caught empty
done

start
caught empty
done
explanation: When the throw happens, the rest of the try block is skipped, so "sent" never prints. Before the exception leaves upload(), the JVM runs that method's finally block, so "cleanup" prints while the exception is still in flight. Only then does the exception reach the caller's catch block, which prints "caught empty", and execution continues normally after the try statement. The rule: finally runs on the way out of its own try, before any outer catch sees the exception.
fixNote: Handle the empty case with an early return; finally still runs.
debugTip: Set an exception breakpoint on IllegalStateException and step over repeatedly; watch the stepper jump into finally before reaching the catch in main.

title: A quantity parser that always says zero
scenario: parseQty should return the parsed number, or 0 if the text is bad. Every valid input comes back as 0 too.
question: What's the root cause?
options: parseInt throws for every input, so catch always runs
The return in finally replaces the try's return value
qty is reset to 0 because it is a local variable
return inside try is ignored when a catch block exists
explanation: A finally block always runs, including after try executes `return qty`. The pending return value is remembered, but if finally completes abruptly with its own return, that new return wins and the old value is discarded. The same thing happens to exceptions: a return in finally silently swallows any exception in flight. That is why most linters flag return (or throw) inside finally; put the fallback after the try statement instead.
fixNote: Move return 0 out of finally to after the try statement.
debugTip: Set a breakpoint on line 6, step over, and watch execution jump to line 10 before leaving the method.

title: Which connection closes first?
scenario: Two resources are opened in one try-with-resources header. Each prints when it opens and closes. Predict the log.
question: What does this print?
options:
open db
open tx
work
close db
close tx
end

open db
open tx
close tx
close db
work
end

open db
open tx
work
close tx
close db
end

open tx
open db
work
close db
close tx
end
explanation: Resources in a try-with-resources header are initialised left to right and closed in the reverse order, like a stack. That matters because later resources often depend on earlier ones: a transaction must be closed before the connection it lives on. close() runs right after the body finishes, before the code after the try statement. The fix shows the equivalent nested form, which makes the reverse order obvious.
fixNote: Equivalent nested form; the order is the same, just explicit.
debugTip: Put breakpoints in close() and look at the call stack each time it is hit to see which resource is being released.
buggyOutput:
open db
open tx
work
close tx
close db
end
fixedOutput:
open db
open tx
work
close tx
close db
end

title: The close failure nobody logged
scenario: The job fails while writing, and the stream also fails when closing. The log only shows the write error, so ops never learn the disk is full.
question: Where did the "disk full" exception go?
options: It replaced the write error, so getMessage is stale
It is attached to the write error as a suppressed exception
close() is never called when the body throws
It was thrown away because only one exception can exist
explanation: When the body throws and close() also throws, try-with-resources keeps the body's exception as the primary one and attaches the close exception to it with addSuppressed. Nothing is lost, but it is only visible through e.getSuppressed() or in a printed stack trace, which shows it under a "Suppressed:" heading. Logging just getMessage() hides it. This is an improvement over a hand-written finally, where the close exception would replace the original one entirely.
fixNote: Loop over e.getSuppressed() and log each one.
debugTip: In the catch block, evaluate `e.getSuppressed()` in the debugger, or log the whole exception with printStackTrace to see the Suppressed section.
fixedOutput:
error: write failed
also: disk full

title: Reading a trace with two exceptions
scenario: Loading a price list crashes. The top of the trace says RuntimeException in load(), but load() only wraps errors.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.RuntimeException: bad row: 2,50
	at Main.load(Main.java:14)
	at Main.main(Main.java:23)
Caused by: java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "2,50"
	at java.base/java.lang.NumberFormatException.forInputString(NumberFormatException.java:67)
	at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:662)
	at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:778)
	at Main.toCents(Main.java:5)
	at Main.load(Main.java:12)
	... 1 more
question: Which line actually failed first?
options: Line 14, where the RuntimeException is created
Line 23, where main prints the list
Line 12, because add() rejects the value
Line 5, the parse shown under "Caused by:"
explanation: A chained exception prints its own frames first, then a "Caused by:" section for the exception passed as the cause. The original failure is the deepest Caused by, and its first Main frame (Main.toCents, line 5) is where things really went wrong: "2,50" still contains a comma after removing dots. The "... 1 more" line means the remaining frames are identical to the outer trace. Always read a chained trace from the bottom-most Caused by upward.
fixNote: Normalise a comma decimal separator before parsing.
debugTip: Read the last "Caused by:" first and jump to its topmost Main frame; or set an exception breakpoint on NumberFormatException.

title: The wrapped error with no cause
scenario: Config errors are wrapped in IllegalStateException. Support asks for the original exception type, but the handler reports the cause as null.
symptom:
bad port: For input string: "80 80"
cause: null
question: Why is the cause null?
options: getCause only works for checked exceptions
Copying the message does not link the original exception
parseInt throws without a stack trace
The catch in main receives a copy of the exception
explanation: Building a new exception from e.getMessage() copies the text but throws away the original object, its type and its stack trace. To keep them, pass the caught exception as the cause argument: new IllegalStateException(msg, e). The cause then appears in getCause() and as a "Caused by:" section in stack traces. Most standard exceptions have a (String, Throwable) constructor for exactly this purpose.
fixNote: Pass e as the cause: new IllegalStateException(msg, e).
debugTip: Breakpoint in main's catch and expand `e` in the variables view; the cause field shows whether the original exception was kept.
buggyOutput:
bad port: For input string: "80 80"
cause: null
fixedOutput:
bad port: 80 80
cause: java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "80 80"

title: An overdraft error with no message
scenario: A custom exception reports why a withdrawal failed. The handler prints the message, but it comes out as null.
question: What's the root cause?
options: The constructor never passes msg to super(msg)
getMessage must be overridden in every subclass
Checked exceptions cannot carry a message
The message is lost when crossing the throws clause
explanation: getMessage() returns the detail message stored by Throwable's constructor. A subclass constructor that does not call super(msg) implicitly calls the no-arg super(), so the stored message is null. Custom exceptions should forward the message (and ideally a cause) to super. Extending Exception makes it checked, which is why withdraw must declare it with throws; extending RuntimeException would make it unchecked.
fixNote: Call super(msg) in the custom exception's constructor.
debugTip: Set a breakpoint after the throw is constructed and inspect the exception's detailMessage field.

title: Every port is the default port
scenario: The server reads its port from settings and falls back to 8080 only if the value is not a number. The setting is "9000", yet it always starts on 8080.
question: What's the root cause?
options: Map.of returns values in an unknown order
A key typo causes an NPE that catch (Exception) hides
8080 is cached as a constant at compile time
parseInt rejects the leading space
explanation: The lookup uses "prot", returns null, and raw.trim() throws NullPointerException. Because the handler catches Exception, the programming error is treated exactly like a bad number and turned into the fallback. Catch the narrowest exception you can actually handle, here NumberFormatException; then a bug like this crashes loudly at the real line instead of silently changing behaviour.
fixNote: Fix the key and catch only NumberFormatException.
debugTip: Breakpoint in the catch block and inspect the type of `e`; seeing NullPointerException instead of NumberFormatException reveals the real problem.

title: A ratio check that still crashes
scenario: ratio() should report bad input and return 0 instead of crashing. It handles text fine, but a zero divisor crashes the program.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero
	at Main.ratio(Main.java:6)
	at Main.main(Main.java:15)
question: Which fix is correct?
options: Catch ArithmeticException too, with a multi-catch
Wrap the division in Integer.valueOf
Move the division into a finally block
Declare throws ArithmeticException on ratio
explanation: Integer division by zero throws ArithmeticException, which is unrelated to NumberFormatException, so the existing catch does not match and the exception escapes. A multi-catch, catch (A | B e), lets one handler cover several unrelated types without catching everything. The alternatives in a multi-catch must not be subclasses of each other, and e is implicitly final. Declaring throws on an unchecked exception changes nothing at runtime.
fixNote: Use catch (NumberFormatException | ArithmeticException e).
debugTip: Set an exception breakpoint for ArithmeticException; it stops on line 6 with y == 0 in the variables view.

title: A crash before the first line of config
scenario: Config holds settings in static fields. Touching Config.PORT crashes with an error that is not the exception you would expect.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError
	at Main.main(Main.java:9)
Caused by: java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "80a"
	at java.base/java.lang.NumberFormatException.forInputString(NumberFormatException.java:67)
	at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:662)
	at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:778)
	at Config.<clinit>(Main.java:3)
	... 1 more
question: What does ExceptionInInitializerError mean here?
options: Config's static initialiser threw while the class loaded
main threw before printing anything
Config.PORT is null because it was not assigned
The JVM could not find the Config class file
explanation: Static field initialisers run once, when the class is first used. If one throws, the JVM wraps the exception in ExceptionInInitializerError, and the real problem appears under "Caused by:" with a <clinit> frame pointing at the failing line. The class is then marked unusable: any later access throws NoClassDefFoundError, which is far more confusing. Keep fallible work out of static initialisers, or validate config explicitly at startup.
fixNote: Use a valid number for the static port value.
debugTip: Read the "Caused by:" section and its <clinit> frame; or set an exception breakpoint on NumberFormatException.

title: File sizes from a manifest
scenario: A manifest lists file sizes in bytes. Small files are fine, but a 3 GB file crashes the parser even though the text is a valid number.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "3000000000"
	at java.base/java.lang.NumberFormatException.forInputString(NumberFormatException.java:67)
	at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:662)
	at java.base/java.lang.Integer.parseInt(Integer.java:778)
	at Main.main(Main.java:6)
question: Why does a valid number fail to parse?
options: parseInt cannot read more than nine digits
total is long, so parseInt must return long
The value overflows int, so parseInt rejects it
The array literal stores the number with a space
explanation: Integer.parseInt throws NumberFormatException not only for non-digits but also for values outside the int range (-2147483648 to 2147483647). 3000000000 is larger than Integer.MAX_VALUE, so the parser refuses it instead of wrapping around. The message still says For input string, which looks like a format problem. Use Long.parseLong (or BigInteger) for values that can exceed 2^31 - 1.
fixNote: Parse with Long.parseLong.
debugTip: Set an exception breakpoint on NumberFormatException and evaluate `s.length()` and `Integer.MAX_VALUE` to compare.

title: The retry that never retries
scenario: fetch() wraps I/O errors so it can be used in lambdas. The caller retries on IOException, but the program crashes on the first failure.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.io.UncheckedIOException: java.io.IOException: timeout
	at Main.fetch(Main.java:9)
	at Main.main(Main.java:18)
Caused by: java.io.IOException: timeout
	... 2 more
question: Why is the failure rethrown?
options: UncheckedIOException is not an IOException; it wraps one
The loop breaks before the catch block runs
instanceof is always false for exceptions
fetch must declare throws IOException to be retried
explanation: IOException is a checked exception: the compiler forces callers to catch or declare it. UncheckedIOException is a RuntimeException that carries an IOException as its cause, so it can escape lambdas and methods without throws clauses. It is not itself an IOException, so the instanceof test fails and the exception is rethrown. Catch UncheckedIOException (and use getCause() for the I/O detail), or unwrap the cause before testing.
fixNote: Catch UncheckedIOException directly.
debugTip: Breakpoint in the catch and evaluate `e.getClass()` and `e.getCause().getClass()`.

title: Timeouts from a legacy loader
scenario: An old helper with raw types fills a Map<String, Integer> of timeouts. The crash happens later, on a line that only reads the map.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ClassCastException: class java.lang.String cannot be cast to class java.lang.Integer (java.lang.String and java.lang.Integer are in module java.base of loader 'bootstrap')
	at Main.main(Main.java:14)
question: What's the root cause?
options: HashMap converts "30" to an Integer on get
get returns null and unboxing fails
Line 14 casts the wrong key type
A raw Map let a String into a Map<String, Integer>
explanation: Generic types are erased at runtime, so a Map<String, Integer> is just a Map to the JVM. Passing it to a raw Map parameter turns off compile-time checking, and put("db", "30") stores a String without complaint (heap pollution). The compiler inserts a hidden cast to Integer where the value is read, so the ClassCastException appears at line 14, far from the real bug. Generics are also invariant for the same safety reason: List<String> is not a List<Object>, and raw types are the loophole.
fixNote: Give the helper a typed parameter and store real Integers.
debugTip: Never suppress unchecked warnings blindly; compile with -Xlint:unchecked, or add a watch on the map's entries right after loadLegacy returns.

title: The largest version number
scenario: A generic max() is used to find the newest build number from a list of strings. Predict what it prints.
question: What does this print?
explanation: The bound T extends Comparable<T> means max can call compareTo, and it uses whatever natural order T defines. For String that order is lexicographic, character by character, so "9" beats "100" and "10" because '9' > '1'. The generic code is correct; the type argument is the problem. Store numbers as Integer (or pass a Comparator) to get numeric ordering.
fixNote: Use List<Integer> so compareTo compares numbers.
debugTip: Add a watch on `x.compareTo(best)` inside the loop and step through each element.

title: A total that drops the cents
scenario: sum() accepts any list of numbers so it works for Integer and Double. Totals of doubles come out too low.
question: What's the root cause?
options: Elements read through the wildcard are only Numbers, and intValue truncates
A List<Double> cannot be passed to sum at all
? extends Number turns Doubles into Integers
double total loses precision after three additions
explanation: List<? extends Number> accepts a List<Integer> or List<Double>, because generics are invariant and the wildcard is what allows subtypes. Reading gives you elements typed as Number, so you only get Number's methods, and intValue() truncates 1.5 to 1. You also cannot add anything but null to such a list: it is a producer (read-only). The PECS rule says: use ? extends for sources you read from, ? super for sinks you write into.
fixNote: Use doubleValue() when summing Numbers.
debugTip: Add a watch on `n` and `n.intValue()` inside the loop to see each fractional part disappear.

title: A discount lookup that crashes on members
scenario: Members get a stored discount; non-members get 0. The ternary crashes for a member whose discount is not in the map yet.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.lang.Integer.intValue()" because the return value of "java.util.Map.get(Object)" is null
	at Main.main(Main.java:10)
question: Why does assigning to an Integer throw NPE?
options: Integer variables cannot hold null
The ternary's type is int, so null is unboxed
println cannot print a null Integer
HashMap.get throws for missing keys
explanation: When one branch of ?: is Integer and the other is the primitive int 0, the whole expression has type int. Java therefore unboxes pct.get(u) by calling intValue() on it, and for "ben" that value is null, giving NullPointerException before anything is assigned. The helpful NPE message even names Integer.intValue(). Make both branches the same reference type, or avoid null with getOrDefault.
fixNote: Use getOrDefault so no null reaches the unboxing.
debugTip: Read the helpful NPE message: it names intValue() and the expression; set a conditional breakpoint on line 10 for u.equals("ben").

title: Version check that fails for big builds
scenario: The app checks whether the installed build matches the server build. It works for build 100 but reports a mismatch for build 1000.
question: What's the root cause?
options: valueOf returns Integer objects, and == compares references
parseInt and valueOf disagree for numbers above 999
Strings longer than three chars are not interned
valueOf rounds 1000 to a cached value
explanation: Integer.parseInt returns a primitive int, while Integer.valueOf returns an Integer object. valueOf reuses cached objects only for -128 to 127, so two calls for 100 give the same object but two calls for 1000 give different objects. == on references checks identity, not value. Use parseInt when you want a number, and equals (or unboxing) when comparing wrapper objects.
fixNote: Parse to primitive int with parseInt and compare with ==.
debugTip: In the debugger, look at the object ids shown for x and y; different ids mean == is false.

title: A blocked user gets through
scenario: Blocked user ids are stored as Long. User 42 is blocked, but the check lets them in.
question: Why is user 42 not found?
options: contains(Object) boxes the int to Integer, which never equals a Long
HashSet hashes Long and int to different buckets randomly
42L and 42 are different numbers in Java
The set must be sorted before contains works
explanation: contains takes an Object, so there is no conversion to Long: the int is autoboxed to Integer. Long.equals returns true only if the argument is also a Long with the same value, so an Integer 42 is never equal to a Long 42, and the last line prints false for the same reason. The compiler does not warn because any Object is allowed. Use the same wrapper type on both sides, here a long id that boxes to Long.
fixNote: Declare the id as long so it boxes to Long.
debugTip: Evaluate `((Object) userId).getClass()` at line 8; it shows Integer, not Long.

title: Digit sum of a mixed code
scenario: digitSum should add up only the digits in a product code like "a1b2". It returns 24 instead of 3.
question: What's the root cause?
options: toCharArray includes a hidden terminator character
getNumericValue gives letters values too: 'a' is 10
getNumericValue returns the char code, like (int) c
sum overflows when letters are added
explanation: Character.getNumericValue is designed for any numeric-looking character, including letters used as digits in bases up to 36, so 'a' is 10 and 'b' is 11 (and it returns -1 for characters with no numeric value). That gives 10 + 1 + 11 + 2 = 24. Filter first with Character.isDigit, or use c - '0' after checking c is between '0' and '9'. The Character class has many such helpers (isLetter, isWhitespace, toUpperCase); read what each actually accepts.
fixNote: Only add characters that pass Character.isDigit.
debugTip: Put a watch on `c` and `Character.getNumericValue(c)` and step through the loop.

title: A path that never gets its slash
scenario: ensureSlash should make sure a folder path ends in "/" before a file name is appended. The final path has no separator.
question: What's the root cause?
options: String concatenation is optimised away by the compiler
The method needs a StringBuilder parameter instead
The method rebinds its own copy of the reference
endsWith is case-sensitive and misses the slash
explanation: Java passes the reference by value: path starts as a copy of dir's reference. path + "/" creates a brand-new String, because Strings are immutable, and assigning it to path changes only the local variable. The caller's dir still points at the original object. Return the new String and reassign it in the caller.
fixNote: Return the new string and assign it back to dir.
debugTip: Step into ensureSlash and watch both `path` and the caller's `dir` in the frames view; only one changes.

title: Logging a password that was never set
scenario: A debug log prints account fields with String.valueOf. The username prints fine, then logging an unset char[] secret crashes.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot read the array length because "value" is null
	at java.base/java.lang.String.<init>(String.java:278)
	at java.base/java.lang.String.valueOf(String.java:4468)
	at Main.main(Main.java:8)
question: Why does one valueOf print null and the other throw?
options: valueOf(char[]) is a different overload that reads the array
Static char arrays are not initialised until used
valueOf throws whenever the argument is null
String concatenation cannot handle char arrays
explanation: Overload resolution happens at compile time on the static type. String.valueOf(user) picks valueOf(Object), which returns "null" for null. String.valueOf(secret) picks the more specific valueOf(char[]), which builds a new String from the array's contents and throws NullPointerException when the array is null. Never print secrets anyway: mask them, and check for null explicitly.
fixNote: Check for null and mask the secret instead of converting it.
debugTip: Step into String.valueOf on line 8 to see which overload the compiler chose.

title: An email template with a mystery gap
scenario: A text block builds an email body and the code prints its length and the body wrapped in brackets. Predict the output.
question: What does this print?
options:
27
[Hi Ana,
Your order shipped.]

30
[Hi Ana,
  Your order shipped.
]

54
[            Hi Ana,
              Your order shipped.
]

28
[Hi Ana,
  Your order shipped.]
explanation: A text block strips incidental indentation: the smallest common indent of its lines, including the line with the closing delimiter, is removed, so "Hi Ana," starts at column 0 while the extra two spaces before "Your" stay. Trailing spaces on each line are also stripped. Because the closing """ is on its own line, the content ends with a newline, which is why the bracket appears on the next line. Put the closing delimiter at the end of the last line to avoid the trailing newline.
fixNote: Close the text block on the last content line to drop the trailing newline.
debugTip: Evaluate `body.chars().filter(c -> c == '\n').count()` or print body with replace("\n", "\\n") to see invisible newlines.

title: A list label missing its bracket
scenario: The builder should produce "[a,b]". The output has the closing bracket but no opening one.
question: What's the root cause?
options: The char '[' is widened to int 91 and used as capacity
StringBuilder trims leading brackets
append(char) skips the first character
println calls toString on an empty builder
explanation: StringBuilder has no constructor taking a char. The char '[' is widened to the int 91, which matches StringBuilder(int capacity), so you get an empty builder with room for 91 characters. Capacity is just the size of the internal buffer; length is the number of characters actually stored. Pass a String, new StringBuilder("["), to set initial content.
fixNote: Use new StringBuilder("[") so it starts with content.
debugTip: Right after line 4, evaluate `sb.length()` and `sb.capacity()`; length 0 with capacity 91 reveals the overload.

title: A CSV row with blank optional fields
scenario: Each row is name,email,phone,notes. When the last fields are empty, reading the notes column crashes.
symptom:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 3 out of bounds for length 2
	at Main.main(Main.java:8)
question: Why does ben's row have fewer fields?
options: split treats ,, as a single separator everywhere
The email contains a dot, which is a regex wildcard
String.join removed the empty values earlier
split removes trailing empty strings by default
explanation: split(regex) is split(regex, 0), and a limit of 0 discards trailing empty strings, so "ben,b@x.io,," yields only 2 elements. Empty strings in the middle are kept; only the trailing ones vanish. Passing a negative limit, split(",", -1), keeps every field; a positive limit caps the number of pieces. String.join, by contrast, keeps empty elements as they are, as the last line would show.
fixNote: Use split(",", -1) to keep trailing empty fields.
debugTip: Set an exception breakpoint on ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException and inspect `f` and `row` when it stops.
fixedOutput:
ana n=4
notes=vip
ben n=4
notes=
x||y

title: A running total that allocates
scenario: The report sums a million readings and gives the right answer, but profiling shows millions of short-lived objects created by this loop.
question: What creates the garbage?
options: i % 7 allocates a new Integer each time
println boxes total at the end of the loop
total += unboxes, adds and boxes a new Long each pass
The underscore literal creates a BigInteger
explanation: total is a Long, an immutable wrapper object. total += x compiles to total = Long.valueOf(total.longValue() + x): unbox, add, then box the result. Only values from -128 to 127 come from the cache, so almost every iteration allocates a new Long. Use primitive long for accumulators and counters, and keep wrappers for collections and nullable values.
fixNote: Declare the accumulator as primitive long.
debugTip: Profile with JFR (jcmd <pid> JFR.start) and look at allocation samples, or decompile with javap -c to see Long.valueOf in the loop.
